title: Roommates
synopsis: Four people, one apartment in Brooklyn, one chore wheel that has, over six months, become a graph theory problem. Tonight's house meeting is about, ostensibly, the dishwasher.

nodes.text: Sunday, 7 p.m. The agenda has been emailed. Item one: dishwasher. Item two: 'something we need to discuss as a group.' Item three: snacks. Marcus has brought, at his own expense, snacks.

choices.text: Open with item three
choices.consequence: Defuse with snacks.

choices.text: Open with item one
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Discipline.

nodes.text: Lola lays out two bags of chips and a cheese plate. The cheese plate has, you realize, four different cheeses for four different roommates. Lola, as always, is the heart of the apartment.

choices.text: Compliment Lola publicly
choices.consequence: “Compliment Lola publicly” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Lift.

choices.text: Eat cheese; save the gratitude
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Eat cheese; save the gratitude” back. Implicit shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

nodes.text: The dishwasher has been stacked badly, every day, for three weeks. Specifically, Bento (who is normally great) has been doing the abominable thing with the small plates.

choices.text: Call Bento out kindly
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Call Bento out kindly” back. Direct shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Show the group a five-minute YouTube video
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Outsourced—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: Bento admits, looking at the floor, that his dad has been sick and he has been distracted. The room rearranges. The dishwasher, suddenly, is the smallest item on the night's true agenda.

choices.text: Reorganize the agenda for Bento
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Pivot—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Keep the agenda; offer Bento support after
choices.consequence: “Keep the agenda; offer Bento support after” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Hybrid.

nodes.text: Lola announces, with rehearsed calm, that her girlfriend Priya might move in. The lease is up in March. The math, suddenly, is different.

choices.text: Engage with the math honestly
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Cost.

choices.text: Engage with Priya as a person first
choices.consequence: Person before lease.

nodes.text: Marcus, who has been quietly considering a move to Berlin, says — out loud, for the first time — 'I might leave in May.' The room, again, shifts. Three big things on the agenda. None of them is, anymore, the dishwasher.

choices.text: Address all three at once
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Comprehensive.

choices.text: Take them one by one
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Sequential—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: Bento brings up, gently, that the apartment cat (Phyllis) is going to need new accommodations if anyone moves. Phyllis is, technically, all of yours. Phyllis is, emotionally, Bento's.

choices.text: Promise Bento that Phyllis stays with him
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Easy.

choices.text: Set up shared visitation if anyone moves
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Custody.

nodes.text: The shared chore spreadsheet has, over six months, mutated into a mood tracker, a snack inventory, and a grudge log. You all look at it together for the first time in a year. It is, terrifyingly, accurate.

choices.text: Archive it and start fresh
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Reset.

choices.text: Audit it column by column
choices.consequence: “Audit it column by column” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Honest.

nodes.text: Lola proposes Tuesday dinners — a guaranteed time you're all in the same room weekly. Marcus, who has a yoga class, hesitates. Bento, who needs this, says 'please.'

choices.text: Make Tuesday a permanent rule
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Routine.

choices.text: Try it for a month first
choices.consequence: You commit to “Try it for a month first.” The story records the instinct as “Trial” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: Priya arrives with a roast chicken she has, somehow, cooked at her own apartment and transported. She is, immediately, the fifth member of the room in a way nobody quite predicted.

choices.text: Vote her in early
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Vote her in early” back. Welcome shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Take six months to vote
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Pace—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: Bento's dad gets a better doctor. The treatment plan is, slowly, working. The room celebrates one Friday with a takeout dinner that costs more than any of you should spend. Nobody minds.

choices.text: Make a tradition of small celebrations
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Make a tradition of small celebrations” back. Mark joy shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Keep it casual; don't formalize joy
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Light—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: Marcus's Berlin plan firms up. He cries at a Tuesday dinner. The cry is, in its own way, the whole apartment saying 'we are about to change.'

choices.text: Plan the goodbye thoughtfully
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Honor it.

choices.text: Plan a visit to Berlin together for the fall
choices.consequence: You commit to “Plan a visit to Berlin together for the fall.” The story records the instinct as “Future-focused” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: Phyllis, ten years old, has a small scare at the vet. She turns out to be fine. The fact that all four of you went to the vet together makes the receptionist laugh.

choices.text: Confirm Phyllis's primary parent is Bento
choices.consequence: “Confirm Phyllis's primary parent is Bento” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Clarify.

choices.text: Decide Phyllis is, in the end, a shared family member
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Shared.

nodes.text: On Marcus's last night you cook the meals he loves and bring out the bottle of wine he saved. Lola makes him a small album of photos. Bento writes him a letter. You hand him a small box.

choices.text: Tell Marcus what he meant to you
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Out loud—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Let the small box speak
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Quiet.

nodes.text: Five months later, three of you visit Marcus in Berlin. He shows you his bakery, his park, his new dumb mustache. You realize the apartment was never just walls. It was the people.

choices.text: Make annual trips a thing
choices.consequence: You commit to “Make annual trips a thing.” The story records the instinct as “Tradition” and carries it forward.

choices.text: Take this trip and let the future be the future
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Present-only.

nodes.text: Priya's stuff arrives in a U-Haul Lola has, somehow, driven in Brooklyn without weeping. The apartment fits her quickly. The new chore wheel includes her in handwriting that is, finally, less aggressive.

choices.text: Move in together permanently as a chosen family
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Build—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Stay flexible; let people come and go
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Stay flexible; let people come and go” back. Open shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

nodes.text: You and Bento, late one night, redesign the spreadsheet with a single sheet titled 'Joy' that just tracks small good moments. The sheet has, by year's end, several hundred entries. You realize the apartment has gotten richer in the kind of math that counts.

choices.text: Show the sheet at New Year's
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Show the sheet at New Year's” back. Share shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Keep the sheet private to the two of you
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Quiet.

nodes.text: You float the idea of an annual roommate trip — three nights, somewhere small. The chat blows up with location ideas. Marcus, in Berlin, requests Sicily. Nobody can afford Sicily. Everyone agrees to a cabin in the Catskills.

choices.text: Plan it now
choices.consequence: Build the tradition.

choices.text: Plan it when energy is higher
choices.consequence: You commit to “Plan it when energy is higher.” The story records the instinct as “Later” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: Phyllis, sixteen, slows down. You take turns sleeping on the couch with her. The apartment becomes a hospice and a celebration at once. You realize the joy sheet has, in this last year, never been more full.

choices.text: Stay in this apartment through the loss
choices.consequence: “Stay in this apartment through the loss” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Honor.

choices.text: Let it be the place that held her, then move
choices.consequence: “Let it be the place that held her, then move” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Move on.

nodes.text: December 31. You and Bento, Lola, Priya, and a FaceTime'd Marcus stand on the roof at 11:58. You decide together what kind of family you'll be next year — the long-haul chosen kind, or the open-door kind that lets people grow.

choices.text: Chosen family, locked in
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Family—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Open door, evolving family
choices.consequence: You commit to “Open door, evolving family.” The story records the instinct as “Open” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: Years later, two of you are at the others' weddings. Three of you co-own a small bakery in Brooklyn. Phyllis lives a long, full cat life. The apartment, when the lease finally ends, is replaced — by all of you, deliberately — with a series of apartments that, in the end, become a network of homes.

Some of you move. Some of you stay. Some of you, years later, drift apart in the ordinary way friends drift. You realize the apartment was a kind of beginning, not a permanent address. You are okay with that. You are, in fact, grateful for it.
